Sample text:
---
The county historical society had hired Julian to bottle a ghost, though the contract called it an *acoustic baseline survey*.

He arrived in the valley of Lower Eldon on a Tuesday in late October, when the sycamores along the creek were dropping leaves the size of dinner plates and the light had already taken on the pale, washed-out quality of early winter. From the overlook at the top of the ridge road, the valley looked like a green-and-ochre bowl tilted slightly toward the east. Down at the bottom, where the Eldon River looped lazily around a shelf of limestone, sat forty-two houses, a brick post office, a hardware store with a faded *Red Man Tobacco* sign painted on its flank, a white clapboard Methodist church, and a cemetery whose oldest stones tilted at the angle of tired teeth.

By April, none of it would be visible from the road. A concrete gravity dam was already nearing completion three miles downstream, where the valley narrowed into a rocky throat. When the sluice gates dropped, the Eldon River would back up, slow down, and spread outward until seventy feet of cold, green water sat over the steeple of the Methodist church.

Someone from the state university had already come through in August with a large-format camera to photograph every facade, porch, and barn door. Someone else had inventoried the headstones and overseen the relocation of the few graves whose descendants had answered the certified letters. But a woman on the heritage board—an eccentric retired music teacher named Mrs. Bellamy—had insisted that photographs were insufficient. Photographs, she had argued at the county commission meeting, made everything look dead before it had even stopped moving. She wanted the sound of the place. She wanted the wind in the cottonwoods, the creak of the suspension footbridge, the bell in the church tower, the water tumbling over the old mill weir.

So Julian drove his battered Subaru wagon down the switchbacks with four Pelican cases in the back, two hundred feet of balanced XLR cable coiled behind the passenger seat, and a notebook full of coordinates.

He parked beside the hardware store and killed the engine. He sat for five minutes without opening the door, letting the ticking of the cooling exhaust manifold fade until the valley’s real floor of sound rose up to meet him.

That was always the first step. People imagined silence as an absence, a blank sheet of paper on which noises were drawn, but in forty-odd years of listening for a living, Julian had never once encountered true silence outside of an anechoic chamber, and even there he had heard the wet thud of his own heart and the high, faint hiss of his nervous system. Out here, what passed for quiet was actually a dense, woven fabric: the dry hiss of tall fescue scraping against itself on the hillside; the far-off, three-note complaint of a crow; the steady, low-frequency shush of the river over gravel beds two hundred yards away; and, underneath it all, a barely perceptible thrum—not quite audible, more like a pressure against the eardrums—from the diesel generators running out at the dam site.

He stepped out into the chill air, zipped his canvas jacket to the chin, and opened the hatchback.

Most of the town had already cleared out. The county had bought the properties at fair market value—a phrase that meant different things depending on whether you were a retired schoolteacher eager for a condo near the hospital in Lexington or a third-generation dairy farmer with forty acres of bottomland—and the deadline for voluntary relocation had passed three weeks ago. Plywood covered the lower windows of the post office. Someone had taken the brass mail drop slot right out of the wall, leaving a neat rectangle of exposed mortar. Across the street, a porcelain sink sat on the front porch of a green bungalow, detached from its pipes like a tooth pulled from a jaw.

Julian rigged his primary setup: a stereo pair of small-diaphragm condenser microphones mounted in a blimp windshield covered in grey synthetic fur—a "dead cat," as the trade called it—perched atop a lightweight carbon-fiber boom. He slung the digital field recorder across his chest, plugged in his closed-back headphones, and pushed the monitoring gain up until the world snapped into sharp, magnified focus.

Through the headphones, the valley grew enormous. The dry rustle of his own jacket sleeve sounded like gravel sliding down a chute. When he took a step on the cracked asphalt of Main Street, the grit beneath his boot soles crackled like fire.

He stood still, holding his breath, and pointed the blimp down the empty street.

A loose sheet of corrugated tin somewhere behind the feed store lifted an inch in a gust of wind and settled back against a rafter with a hollow, metallic *thrum-clack*. Two seconds later, the echo of it returned off the limestone bluff on the far side of the creek, softer and rounder, stripped of its sharp edges. A sparrow hopped along the rain gutter of the hardware store, each tiny claw scratching the galvanized metal with astonishing clarity.

Julian hit the red record button, watched the timecode begin to roll, and stood completely motionless for six full minutes.

That was the discipline of the work, and also the boredom of it, though Julian rarely found it boring. You couldn't fidget. You couldn't clear your throat or shift your weight from one foot to the other. You had to become a piece of furniture on the street, waiting for the place to forget you were there and resume its own conversation.

By noon, he had captured the interior acoustics of the abandoned post office—a tight, boxy room that still smelled faintly of damp paper and floor wax, where a single drop of water from a leaking roof flashing fell into a bucket every eleven seconds with a musical, rising *plink*—and the hollow groan of the wooden deck on the footbridge over the creek.

It was at the Methodist church that he realized he was being watched.

The church doors weren't locked; the county crew had pulled the padlock hasp off the frame when they hauled out the pews and the upright piano, leaving the sanctuary gutted down to its pine floorboards. Julian had propped the microphone stand dead center in the empty nave and climbed the narrow, steep stairs to the belfry, hoping the rope was still attached to the cast-iron bell. It was, though frayed and stiff with age. He planned to set the recorder running downstairs, come back up, or pull the rope gently from the vestibule—not a full peal, just enough to wake the bronze and let it ring out into the empty rafters.

When he came back down the stairs, squinting against the dimness after the bright dust of the belfry, a man was standing in the open doorway.

He was tall and slightly stooped, wearing faded denim overalls over a plaid flannel shirt, with a canvas cap pulled down over sparse white hair. In his left hand he held a galvanized bucket half-full of black walnuts.

"Didn't think there was anybody left down here except the scrappers," the man said. His voice was gravelly, pitched low, and in the stripped-out sanctuary it bounced off the bare plaster walls and hung in the air for a long second.

Julian slid his headphones down around his neck. "County historical society," he said, stepping carefully around his mic cables. "I'm recording the town. Sounds, mostly."

The man looked at the furry grey blimp on its stand in the middle of the floor, then up at Julian's face. His eyes were a pale, watery blue, set deep under bristling eyebrows.

"Recording," he repeated, as if testing the word to see if it held weight. "You're taking pictures of noise."

"Something like that."

"Well, you're a little late," the man said, setting the walnut bucket down on the threshold. "Should've been here thirty years ago when the Saturday night dance was going at the Grange hall. Or when the sawmill had its whistle. Ain't nothing making a sound worth keeping now except the wind, and the wind'll still be here after they fill the hole."

"I'm Julian," he said, offering a hand.

The man shook it once, firmly. His palm felt like cured leather. "Hollis Vance. Live up the hollow about half a mile, past the old creamery."

"I thought everyone was out by the first of the month."

"Most everybody," Hollis said. "My deed had an extension till December first. Had to argue with a kid in a suit from Frankfort for three months to get it, too. Told him I wasn't moving sixty years of machine tools in three weeks just so some bass fishermen from Cincinnati could have a place to troll earlier in the spring. They gave me till the frost sets in hard."

Julian glanced back at his recorder. The little amber peak lights were pulsing gently as Hollis shifted his weight on the dry floorboards. "Mind if I ask what kind of machine tools?"

"Lathe, milling machine, old forging press, couple of grinders," Hollis said. "Used to repair farm equipment. Tractors, balers, whatever broke before harvest. Ain't much farming left around here the last ten years anyway, mostly just fixing mowers and welding gates, but a man likes his shop."

He looked up toward the ceiling, where a square hole let the bell rope drop down into the vestibule. "You going to ring that thing?"

"If it'll move," Julian said. "Mrs. Bellamy at the historical society specifically asked for it."

Hollis let out a short, dry bark of a laugh. "Clara Bellamy. She hasn't set foot in this church since her sister's funeral in ninety-eight. Tell you what—don't yank it hard. The yoke bolts are half rusted through. Pull it slow, let the clapper kiss the lip once. That's all it needs."

Julian went back to the recorder, checked his input levels—giving himself plenty of headroom so the bell wouldn't clip the preamps—and walked back to the vestibule. He took hold of the hemp rope. It felt cold and fibrous, shedding tiny splinters of chaff onto his palms. He pulled steadily downward.

Above them, iron groaned against weathered oak. Then, a single, monumental *bong* dropped through the ceiling—not bright and celebratory, as a church bell sounds on a Sunday morning, but heavy, slightly flat, and rich with complex overtones that seemed to vibrate right inside Julian's sternum. The sound filled the stripped nave, rattled a loose pane of wavy glass in the west window, spilled out the open door into the yard, and rolled across the valley toward the creek.

Even after the fundamental note died away, a ghostly hum lingered in the room for ten, fifteen, twenty seconds, decaying slowly back into the rustle of the autumn grass outside.

Julian waited until the meters on his recorder dropped all the way back to the baseline before he let out his breath.

Hollis hadn't moved from the doorway. He stood looking out across the dry churchyard toward the row of maples bordering the road.

"That's her," Hollis said quietly. "First time she's rung since they hauled the pews out last month. Sounds hollow without the carpet."

"Everything sounds different when you empty a room," Julian said. "You lose all the soft surfaces. No curtains, no cushions, no coats. The sound has nowhere to go except back into the walls."

Hollis picked up his bucket of walnuts. "You want to hear something that still has its furniture in it, come on up to my place around four. Got a pot of coffee on the stove. You can record my kettle if you're hard up for material."

---

Hollis Vance’s house sat where the valley floor began to pinch upward into a narrow wooded draw, far enough back from the main road that you couldn't see it until you crossed a timber bridge over a feeder branch. Beside the neat two-story farmhouse stood a long, low building made of cinderblock and corrugated siding, with a tall stovepipe jutting from its roof like a periscope.

A blue column of hickory smoke rose straight up from the pipe into the windless late-afternoon air.

Julian arrived just after four. The sun had already dropped behind the western ridge, plunging the hollow into a cool blue shadow while the tips of the highest oaks up on the rim still burned bright copper. He left the bulky blimp in the car and brought only a pair of small omnidirectional microphones and a handheld recorder. People froze up when you pointed a huge furry zeppelin at their faces; they acted like they were on television, clearing their throats and trying to say profound things. Small mics left on a workbench were easier to forget.

Inside, the shop smelled wonderfully of cutting oil, warm cast iron, damp concrete, and woodsmoke. Every inch of wall space was organized with the quiet fanaticism of a man who had never thrown away a bolt that still had threads on it. Coffee cans full of washers sat neatly labeled on sagging pine shelves. An ancient South Bend lathe occupied the center of the concrete floor, draped in a heavy canvas tarp, ready to be winched onto a flatbed trailer. Beside it, a potbellied coal stove radiated a dry, steady heat that made Julian's chilled knuckles ache pleasantly as he peeled off his gloves.

Hollis was sitting on a three-legged stool by the workbench, scraping the green husks off his walnuts with an old pocketknife and dropping the ridged brown shells into a burlap sack. His fingers were stained nearly black with juglone.

"Pull up a crate," he said, nodding toward an upturned milk box near the stove. "Mugs are on the shelf behind the drill press."

Julian poured himself black coffee from a speckled enamel pot sitting directly on the stove's flat top. It tasted slightly burnt and entirely restorative. He asked permission before setting his two small mics down on a stack of shop rags at the far end of the bench, spacing them about seven inches apart—roughly the width of a human head—to capture a natural stereo image.

"Just pretend they're salt shakers," Julian said, tapping the record button and tucking the little box beside a grease gun.

"They look like bugs," Hollis muttered, though he went right back to his walnuts.

For a while, neither of them said anything. The shop had its own small orchestra. The fire shifted inside the stove with a soft collapse of embers, followed by the faint, high-pitched *tink-tink* of the sheet-metal stovepipe expanding. Outside, the feeder creek babbled over slate ledges. Somewhere in the rafters, a mud dauber's nest detached a crumb of dried clay that hit the concrete floor like a grain of sand. And every few seconds came the crisp, wet *scritch* of Hollis's knife blade separating husk from shell, followed by the dull *thump* of the nut hitting the bottom of the burlap sack.

"You do this a lot?" Hollis asked eventually, without looking up. "Going around before they tear things down?"

"Sometimes," Julian said, wrapping his hands around the warm mug. "Mostly I work for film crews—nature documentaries, independent movies, things like that. Getting clean background tracks so actors don't sound like they're talking in a broom closet. Sometimes museum exhibits. Once I spent two weeks in Montana recording old grain elevators before they tore them down."

"What for?"

Julian thought about how to answer that honestly. The easy answer was *preservation*, the word Mrs. Bellamy liked to use, as if storing a sound on a solid-state drive kept the thing itself alive. The truth was slipperier.

"People forget how places felt," Julian said. "You look at an old photograph of a street, and your brain fills in silence, because photographs don't move. Or worse, your brain fills in whatever noise you're hearing right now—highway traffic, air conditioners. You lose the texture of the air. A sound recording puts you back inside the room. If you listen with your eyes closed, your brain thinks you're standing there."

Hollis stopped scraping for a moment and leaned back on his stool, eyeing the two tiny black cylinders resting on his shop rags.

"Seems cruel to me," he said mildly.

"Cruel?"

"Sure. You take a fellow who grew up down there in Lower Eldon—maybe he moved off to Ohio twenty years ago to work in a tire plant. Now they flood the place. You put a pair of earphones on him in some museum and play him the church bell and the creek. He can't go back there. All you're doing is reminding him of something he can't touch."

Julian looked down into his coffee. He had heard variations of that argument before, mostly from himself at two in the morning while editing waveforms on a laptop screen. There was something faintly voyeuristic about archiving loss—like taking notes at a bedside.

"Maybe," Julian said. "Or maybe it's proof. That it wasn't just a line on a topographical map before it became a lake."

Hollis snorted softly and picked up another walnut. "We know it was here. Don't need a tape to prove my granddaddy built the crib on that barn down by the bend." He pared away a strip of bruised green rind. "You want a real sound of this valley, stay till six-fifteen. Wait till the wind drops right after dark."

"What happens at six-fifteen?"

"The CSX coal drag comes through the gap four miles north," Hollis said, nodding toward the ceiling as if pointing through the roof to the ridge behind the house. "You can't see the tracks from anywhere in Eldon. Never could. Whole mountain ridge in between. But right around dusk, when the cold air sinks down off the oaks and settles in the bottom here, it acts like a lid on a pot. Sound hits that limestone cliff on the east side and bounces right down the hollow. You hear the horn blow for the Miller Crossing three miles away, and then for about four minutes you can hear those locomotives climbing the grade—just this long, low rumble coming right up through the soles of your boots. Used to set my watch by it when I was out cutting firewood."

Julian leaned forward slightly. "How long has that train been running?"

"Longer than me," Hollis said. "Used to be steam when I was a boy. Now it's three diesels pulling a hundred and twenty cars of black rock. Doesn't matter what pulls it. The hill makes it work hard, and the valley carries the groan."

They sat together until five-thirty, talking only in fragments—about the dry summer they'd had, about where Hollis was moving (a two-acre parcel with a pole barn outside Danville, near his daughter's place, flat land with no limestone bluffs to bounce anything back), about the stubbornness of old oak floorboards. When Julian finally picked up his small mics and checked the screen, he had forty-eight minutes of uninterrupted room tone: stove, knife, kettle, footsteps, and two men saying very little.

Before leaving, he asked if he could come back down to the river near the old mill weir later that night to run an overnight rig.

"It's county land now," Hollis said, walking him to the shop door. "Nobody's going to chase you off except maybe a raccoon. Just watch your footing on the weir rocks. Moss gets slick once the dew drops."

At six-ten, Julian parked down near the creek bottom, got his big parabolic dish and stereo rig out, and set them facing the eastern limestone bluff. He put his headphones on, dialed up the gain, and waited.

At six-sixteen, right on schedule, it arrived.

First came a ghostly, mournful chord—a Leslie three-chime horn blown for a grade crossing miles out of sight, stretched and softened by distance until it sounded less like a warning and more like a brass instrument played under water. Thirty seconds later, the floor of the valley began to vibrate. It wasn't a sharp noise; it was a deep, rhythmic *chug-chug-chug* around forty hertz, pulsing steadily as three heavy locomotives clawed their way up the two-percent grade on the far side of the mountain. The sound didn't come from the north; it seemed to leak out of the limestone wall directly in front of him, pouring down into the dark bowl of Eldon like cold water filling a basin.

Julian stood beside his tripod in the gathering dark, shivering inside his jacket, listening through his headphones as the phantom train climbed and climbed, faded into a faint rumble indistinguishable from distant thunder, and finally vanished altogether.

When it was gone, the valley felt twice as wide and twice as lonely.

---

He slept poorly in the back of the Subaru, curled on a foam pad between his equipment cases, waking every hour or two to check the battery levels on the overnight rig he had left down by the river.

Around two in the morning, unable to sleep anymore for the cold seeping up through the floorboards, he pulled on his wool socks and boots, climbed out into the black, frost-stiffened grass, and walked down to the bank with a flashlight tucked under his arm.

The sky had cleared completely. Above the dark silhouettes of the ridges, the Milky Way lay like a smudge of chalk across slate. No porch lights burned anywhere in Lower Eldon. For the first time in a century and a half, there wasn't a single bulb glowing in any of the forty-two houses—not even up the hollow at Hollis's place, where the old man had presumably banked the stove and gone to bed hours ago.

Julian had sunk two hydrophones—waterproof microphones sealed in brass housings—into the pool just below the mill weir, weighted down with river cobbles so the current wouldn't knock them against the bank. Above them, on the gravel bar, a second pair of microphones sat aimed into the sycamore canopy. Both pairs fed into a four-track recorder tucked inside a waterproof dry-bag beneath an upturned canoe someone had abandoned in the brush.

He crouched beside the bag, plugged his headphones into the monitor jack, and switched between the upper and lower channels.

Above water, the night was crisp and sparse. A dry breeze moved high through the crowns of the trees, barely touching the gravel bar. Once, far up the hollow, a barred owl asked its eight-syllable question—*who cooks for you, who cooks for you-all*—and got no answer. Every few minutes, a single sycamore leaf would let go of its twig, spin downward through the dark branches with tiny dry taps, and land with a soft *shh* on the stones.

Then he flipped the monitor switch to the hydrophones.

Underwater, the valley was roaring.

It was astonishing, every single time he did it—that sudden plunge through the surface tension into a completely different acoustic universe. What sounded from the bank like a gentle, sleepy trickle over mossy rocks became, six inches beneath the surface, a turbulent roar like a crowded subway station. Millions of tiny air bubbles hissed and popped continuously as the water tumbled over the weir crest. Beneath the hiss came a steady, percussive knocking—*clack, tick, clack*—as the current rolled grains of quartz and pebbles along the riverbed like marbles in a jar. Once, something heavy and muffled brushed directly past the left hydrophone casing—a submerged branch, perhaps, or a snapping turtle shifting in the mud before winter dormancy.

And beneath all of it, traveling effortlessly through the dense medium of the water even more clearly than through the air, was the low, mechanical hum from three miles downstream.

The dam builders ran shifts around the clock, pouring concrete under floodlights to beat the winter freeze. Down here in the dark pool below the mill, untouched by any light, the sound of those generators and pumps was already inside the river, humming through the limestone shelf like a warning whispered down a pipe.

Julian sat back on his heels on the cold gravel, keeping the headphones pressed against his ears.

He thought about Hollis's accusation in the workshop: *All you're doing is reminding him of something he can't touch.*

Julian didn't know if Mrs. Bellamy's museum exhibit would ever even be built. County budgets shrank; heritage boards turned over; hard drives sat unindexed in filing cabinets in the basements of courthouses while the people who commissioned them forgot what was on them. In ten years, the files he was making tonight—forty-eight kilohertz, twenty-four-bit WAVs labeled cleanly with date, time, GPS coordinates, and microphone spacing—might sit on an institutional server somewhere in Frankfort, listened to once by an intern and never opened again.

Even if someone did listen, Hollis was right: you couldn't bottle a place. A recording was just a shadow cast sideways—an impression left in the mud after the deer had already jumped the fence.

And yet, sitting there with his knees aching from the frost, listening to the gravel knock softly along the bottom of the Eldon River while the generators hummed downstream, Julian felt an intense, quiet certainty that the listening itself mattered, even if the archive didn't. Somebody had to stand still in the dark long enough to notice what was leaving. Somebody had to pay attention to the way the walnut shells dropped into the burlap sack, and the way the limestone cliff caught the train horn at dusk, and the way an empty church held onto a single ring of iron until the air itself gave out.

He took the headphones off and let the natural night rush back into his ears—smaller, colder, less magnified, but whole. Above the ridge, a sliver of moon was rising, pale as a paring of ice.

---

By nine the next morning, Julian had packed the last of his Pelican cases into the wagon.

The frost had come down hard just before dawn, turning every dead goldenrod stalk and barbed-wire fence along the road white and brittle. As the sun finally cleared the eastern ridge, a thick white mist began rising off the river, curling through the empty yards of Lower Eldon and wrapping around the porch columns of the boarded-up houses. From halfway up the switchback road, it looked already as though the water had started to rise, swallowing the hardware store and the church foundation in pale, slow-moving vapor.

Before leaving the valley for good, Julian drove back up the narrow lane past the old creamery and stopped at the timber bridge.

Hollis was out in the yard beside his shop, wrestling a heavy canvas tarp over a pallet of cast-iron gears. His breath plumed white in the morning sun. When he saw the Subaru, he stopped, tucked a loose bungee cord into his belt, and walked down to the edge of the bridge.

"Heading back to the city?" Hollis asked, leaning his forearms on the wooden rail.

"Back to Louisville," Julian said, rolling the window all the way down. The air smelled sharply of woodsmoke and wet frost. "Got about six hours of tape to sort through and label."

"You get your train?"

"Got it," Julian said. "Right at six-sixteen, just like you said. Rattled right off the cliff."

Hollis nodded once, looking satisfied, as if he had personally arranged the schedule. "That ridge is good for something, anyway. Won't be long before the water covers the bottom third of it, though. Reckon that'll change how it bounces."

"Probably," Julian said. "Water reflects high frequencies differently than grass and trees. Might make it brighter, actually, before it gets too deep."

He reached over to the passenger seat and picked up a small padded envelope he had slipped a business card into—not his professional card, just a scrap of heavy paper with his home address and phone number written in ink.

"If you decide you ever want to hear any of it," Julian said, holding it out the window, "once you get settled over in Danville. Drop me a line. I'll burn you a disc or send you a little player with headphones."

Hollis looked at the envelope for a long moment. His hands stayed resting on the weathered oak of the bridge rail. Then, slowly, he took it and slid it into the chest pocket of his overalls.

"Might do that," he said, though both of them knew he almost certainly wouldn't. A man who didn't want his tools rushed wasn't going to sit in a pole barn in Danville listening to a ghost river in a pair of plastic earphones. "Drive careful going up the grade. Frost stays slick in the shade around that third hairpin."

"I will," Julian said. "Good luck with the move, Hollis."

"It's just iron," Hollis said, stepping back from the car and raising two fingers from the brim of his cap. "Heavy as hell, but it moves."

Julian put the wagon in gear and eased back down the lane toward the main road. In his rearview mirror, he watched Hollis turn back toward the cinderblock shop, disappearing behind the corner of the woodpile just before the trees closed off the view.

At the bottom of the valley, Julian didn't stop again. He drove straight through the mist hanging over Main Street, past the gutted church with its crooked lightning rod and the hardware store with its faded tobacco sign, and began the long, winding climb up the switchbacks toward the ridge.

Halfway up, he rolled his window down an inch just to hear the road tires humming on the cold asphalt. Near the top, where the overlook sat, he pulled off onto the gravel shoulder for one last look back.

The mist had thickened now, filling the bowl of the valley completely from ridge to ridge, flat and still and bright silver under the mid-morning sun. Nothing poked through it except the very tip of the Methodist steeple, a tiny white needle floating on a silent sea.

Julian sat in the idling car for thirty seconds, listening to nothing except the faint tick of the heater fan, and then pulled back onto the highway heading west.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A carefully paced literary story uses a sound recordist’s work in a soon-to-be-flooded town to explore what preservation can and cannot save.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient and richly sensory, especially attuned to how sound changes with distance, rooms, water, and listeners. Its pathos comes less from dramatic confrontation than from the slow inventory of a place being emptied: the removed mail slot, the gutted church, Hollis’s tools, the train heard through the valley. The story gives real weight to Hollis’s objection that recordings may sharpen loss rather than ease it, then lets Julian’s quiet conviction coexist with that objection instead of defeating it. It invites the reader to practice the same attention Julian does—and to feel the tenderness and inadequacy of trying to keep what is disappearing.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds a community displaced by a dam, the textures of ordinary work and local sound, and the ethics of turning a place into an archive. Recurring objects—the bell, walnut shells, train, river, and recording equipment—make listening a form of witness while keeping the question of whether witness is enough unresolved. The closing image of the steeple tip above the mist gives the loss a visual counterpart to the sounds Julian has tried to preserve.

## Evidence line
> Somebody had to stand still in the dark long enough to notice what was leaving.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sample’s coherent, distinctive attention to sensory detail and its sustained moral tension make it revealing, while its polished literary-fiction form shapes that evidence.
